title: Discovering needs and qualifying a prospect without pressure
audience: Owners, managers and staff in any service business who talk with prospects about buying a service.
learningOutcomes: Ask needs-discovery questions that uncover a prospect's goal, why it matters and what has stood in the way before, and record the answers
Qualify a prospect honestly on need, budget, schedule and readiness, including a clear decision not to proceed
Present one option and invite a decision, and accept a not-now answer with a recorded follow-up date

instruction.heading: Selling is an honest offer you can ask for
instruction.body: Service providers need to be at ease requesting payment from a prospect for the service. Asking is part of the work, and it is not the same thing as pressure. The honest version is a clear offer, a fair price and a plain question about whether the prospect wants it. Good service also makes the provider a guide, who helps the prospect choose what suits them. That may mean recommending a smaller start, or a different provider.

instruction.heading: Find the need before you describe the service
instruction.body: People often decide on feelings and then explain the decision with facts, so the most useful early question concerns what the person wants and why it matters to them. Ask open questions. What goal has been on your mind? For how long has that goal been with you? Why does it matter now? What has got in the way before? Listen, then reflect back, in your own words, what you heard. The aim is to describe a service that fits what this person wants, not to steer them towards a yes.

instruction.heading: Qualify honestly, including a clear no
instruction.body: Qualification means checking the fit before you sell. Four checks help. Does the service meet the need you have heard? Can the person afford the option you would recommend? Can they keep to the times you offer? Are they ready to put in the effort? If the answer to any of these is no, say so plainly, and refer the person to a suitable option, a later start or a different provider. Before you send any offer, also confirm the work involved, your own capacity, the deadline and the payment terms. Business Queensland's guidance on preparing quotes suggests not quoting for work you cannot deliver to the customer's satisfaction. After a first full session, four plain questions help: did the session suit you, do you want to carry on, is the cost workable for you, and which day suits the next booking? These are honest checks, not a closing script.

instruction.heading: Present the option, and accept the answer
instruction.body: Describe the option by its outcome, what is included, the price, how many sessions are involved, the timing and the cancellation terms. Explaining the benefits before the price, and why the price is what it is, reduces the chance of losing the prospect on price alone. A programme differs from a set of separate sessions. It moves each session towards a stated goal, and its start and finish use the same measures, so that progress can be shown. Then ask for the decision. If the answer is not now, agree a follow-up date and channel, record both, and keep to them. A timed follow-up, with a request for feedback if the prospect does not go ahead, shows which part of the offer did not justify the price. Do not repeat the same request on every contact.

instruction.heading: Keep the emotional side honest
instruction.body: Empathy is a skill. Name the feeling you heard, such as frustration or worry about starting again, and show that you understand it. Do not use fear, false deadlines or invented scarcity, and do not promise results you cannot show. Check every statement about price, savings, results or availability against evidence before you make it. Where a single price is advertised, the ACCC's advertising and selling guide (dated July 2021; confirm it is the current version) indicates that it should include the total, with any tax, fee or levy. Consumer law may apply to how a service is sold, so check the rules that apply in your state or territory and with the ACCC.

procedure: Ask the prospect what goal they want, in their own words, and why it matters now
Ask what has stopped them before, and listen without judging
Run the four qualification checks: need, budget, schedule and readiness
Summarise what you heard, and check the summary with the prospect
Present one option with its outcome, price, sessions, timing and terms
Ask for a decision, and accept a not-now answer with a recorded follow-up date
Record the discovery notes, the qualification result and the outcome

workedExamples.situation: Sam, 44, has not exercised for two years and books a discovery call. He says he wants to get fit. In the conversation he says he wants to keep up with his children at weekends, that he stopped last year because the first months were too tiring to keep up with, and that he cannot fit sessions in before work.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the provider do next, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: The provider should confirm the goal in Sam's words, ask what made the earlier attempt hard, and check that the early-morning slot does not fit. An honest offer may be a short programme in the late afternoon, with a review date and a clear statement of price and cancellation terms. The provider records the goal, the earlier barrier, the schedule constraint and the review date. If the times cannot work, the provider refers Sam to another provider or a later start. Health screening for a first-time client is a separate step, covered in “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries” for personal trainers.

workedExamples.situation: A prospect loves the first session but says she can afford one session a fortnight. The provider's usual package is weekly.
workedExamples.reasoning: The provider should not sell a weekly package the prospect cannot pay for. The honest options are a fortnightly plan with a stated outcome and a review, a shorter starter block, or a referral if the fit is poor. The provider states the price and what it includes, and writes the agreed next step down, so the prospect can decide without pressure.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is needed for this lesson
The current price list and terms of trade

commonErrors.error: Asking questions designed to get a yes, rather than to learn the goal
commonErrors.prevention: Ask open questions, and let the prospect give the answer in their own words.

commonErrors.error: Selling a package the prospect cannot afford
commonErrors.prevention: Run the budget check before you present a price.

commonErrors.error: Repeating the request after a not-now answer
commonErrors.prevention: Agree a follow-up date and channel, record them, and keep to them.

commonErrors.error: Promising results or availability that are not true
commonErrors.prevention: Check every claim against evidence before you say it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Follow-up by email or text can be a commercial electronic message. ACMA's guidance on avoiding spam (read 2026-11-03) says the sender needs consent, must identify itself accurately, and must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within five working days. That page does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check the Spam Act 2003 (Cth) text before sending follow-up messages.
A professional code of ethics is referenced in the source manual but was not read for this lesson. Check which code, if any, applies to you in Australia before you rely on it.

qualityStandard: Discovery notes record the prospect's goal in their own words, the barrier and the timing
Each qualification decision (proceed, adjust or refer) is recorded with reasons
No pressure tactic, false deadline or unverified claim appears in the offer
A not-now answer leads to a recorded follow-up date
documentationEvidence: The offer as presented, with price, inclusions and terms
summary: Asking for a decision is part of the job, and pressure is not
Find the goal and the barrier before describing a service
Qualify on need, budget, schedule and readiness, and say no plainly when the fit is poor
Accept a not-now, record the follow-up date, and use only the channel agreed

knowledgeChecks.question: A prospect says they need to think about it. Which response fits honest selling?
options: Confirm what they are weighing, agree a follow-up date, and record it
Repeat the offer every day until they decide and call them each morning
Tell them the price is going up tomorrow so they should decide today

knowledgeChecks.question: Why ask a prospect how long they have held a goal?
options: To guarantee the sale on the day and to close the sale before lunch
To learn what the goal means to them, so the offer fits what they want
To collect data for a third party and to pass their details to a partner

knowledgeChecks.question: A prospect cannot fit the times you have available. What does honest qualification require?
options: Sell a package anyway and sort out the times later once the client has paid
Tell them the time slot is nearly gone and that the package ends this week
Say so, and refer them on, or suggest a later start if it truly suits them

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages cannot be sent without the recipient's permission or consent; messages must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option under the Spam Act 2003, which the page says sets out responsibilities under Australian law. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Advertising and selling guide: A guide for business
officialReferences.covers: Says a single advertised price should state the total price and include any tax, duty, fee, levy or other additional charges, with optional charges that cannot be quantified as the main exception. Does not address minimum or call-out charges, which remain UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: ACCC.
